**Hanuman**
The monkey god of Hindu myth and the most loyal devotee of Rama in the Ramayana. He is the son of the wind god Vayu and Anjana, and he is the most common giveaway for monkeys.

**Vanaras**
The race of monkey-like (sometimes described as ape-like) forest beings in the Ramayana, said to have been created to help Rama. Hanuman, Sugriva, Vali, Nala and Nila are all vanaras.

**Carrying the mountain of herbs for Lakshmana**
When Rama's brother Lakshmana was gravely wounded in battle, Hanuman was sent to fetch a healing herb (sanjeevani) from the Himalayas. Unable to tell which plant it was, he lifted the whole mountain and carried it back to Lanka.

**Sugriva and the kingdom of Kishkindha**
Sugriva is the king of the vanaras, who live in the forest kingdom of Kishkindha. Rama helped him regain his throne, and in return Sugriva's monkey army helped rescue Sita from the demon king Ravana.

**Vali and the demon Mayavi**
Vali, Sugriva's older brother, chased the demon Mayavi into a cave, and Sugriva, thinking Vali was dead, sealed the cave and took the throne. Vali escaped and drove Sugriva out, until Rama killed Vali, after which Sugriva married Vali's widow Tara. Vali had a boon that gave him half the strength of anyone he fought.

**Rama Setu (Adam's Bridge) to Lanka**
The vanara army built a bridge across the sea to Lanka so Rama could reach Ravana's kingdom and rescue Sita. It was built by Nala and Nila, whose boon meant that any stone they put in the water would float.

**Burning Lanka with his tail**
When Hanuman leapt across the sea to find Sita, Ravana's men captured him and set his tail on fire. Hanuman escaped and used his burning tail to set the city of Lanka ablaze.

**Trying to swallow the sun**
As a child, Hanuman mistook the sun for a ripe fruit and leapt up to eat it. Indra struck him with his thunderbolt (vajra) on the jaw, which gave him his name ("hanu" means jaw), and Vayu withdrew the air from the world in anger until the gods revived Hanuman and gave him boons.

**Hanuman Chalisa**
A devotional hymn of forty verses (chalisa means forty) praising Hanuman, written by the poet Tulsidas. It is one of the most widely recited Hindu prayers.

**Sun Wukong in Journey to the West**
The Monkey King of Chinese myth, born from a stone, who wields a magic staff that can change size. In the novel Journey to the West, he protects the monk Xuanzang (Tripitaka) on his pilgrimage to India, along with Pigsy (Zhu Bajie) and Sandy (Sha Wujing). Some scholars think he was inspired by Hanuman.

**Hanuman tearing open his chest**
To prove his devotion, Hanuman ripped open his chest to reveal images of Rama and Sita in his heart. He also defeated the demon Kalanemi, who disguised himself as a sage to stop Hanuman's search for the healing herb.

**Three wise monkeys**
Mizaru, Kikazaru and Iwazaru, the monkeys who "see no evil, hear no evil, speak no evil." A famous carving of them is at the Toshogu shrine in Nikko, Japan.

**Dream on Monkey Mountain**
A play by the Saint Lucian writer Derek Walcott. Its main character, the charcoal burner Makak (named for the macaque monkey), is jailed by Corporal Lestrade alongside the thieves Souris and Tigre and has visions of returning to Africa.

**"Interpreter of Maladies"**
In Jhumpa Lahiri's short story, Mrs. Das drops a trail of puffed rice that leads a group of monkeys to attack her son Bobby, whom she has confessed was fathered by another man.

**Monkeys in Asian folktales**
In Tibetan myth, the first Tibetans were born from the union of a monkey and a rock ogress (demoness). In the Japanese folktale of the crab and the monkey (Saru Kani Gassen), a monkey kills a crab and is later killed in revenge by the crab's children and their allies.
